title: Ivo and the Portrait
premise: Xanthe Eriksen returns to the decaying family farmhouse to bury his twin sister Wren — except the body in the casket is not Wren's. Seven years after fleeing home, he finds the house unchanged, the noises in the walls louder than ever, and on the porch sits Ivo, the imaginary friend from childhood, untouched by time. Ivo leads Xanthe to a hidden portrait of a boy painted in 1974, the year their great-uncle vanished, and reveals that the thing wearing Wren's face is not Wren at all: it is what took her, and it needs Xanthe's consent to stay. To free his sister's soul and end the family bargain struck in 1974, Xanthe must return the portrait — and the name written on its back — to the well behind the barn before the harvest moon rises, choosing truth over the comforting lie that kept him belonging to this family.
about_author: Tamsin Thornbury grew up on a failing orchard farm in rural Vermont, where she swears the cellar door was always warm to the touch. She writes horror about families who mistake inheritance for love, and lives with two cats who refuse to enter one particular room.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the funeral home, Xanthe lifts the casket lid and sees his own face — aged, wrong — where Wren's should be. The funeral director insists nothing is amiss. Emotional beat: grief curdling into dread; the first crack in seven years of denial.

chapters.title: Homecoming
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He drives to the Eriksen farmhouse through dying orchards, noting every gate and fence post exactly as it was when he fled at nineteen. His mother greets him warmly, too warmly, and asks why he came back 'so soon.' Beat: the uncanny comfort of a place that never changed.

chapters.title: Noises Have Explanations
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, night one. Scratching inside the walls, footsteps above the ceiling of a single-story house. He catalogs rational explanations aloud like a ritual. In the morning, the explanations are gone from his notebook, replaced by tally marks. Beat: denial as survival strategy beginning to fail.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. On the porch sits Ivo — the imaginary friend, a lanky figure with button eyes and a stitched smile — unchanged since childhood, while Xanthe has grown. No one else can see him. Ivo says only: 'You brought it back with you.' Beat: terror braided with relief at being seen.

chapters.title: Mother Knows Best
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. His mother serves dinner for three, setting a plate for Wren, who 'is resting.' When Xanthe mentions the casket, her face goes smooth as poured wax. Upstairs, something answers to Wren's voice. Beat: loyalty to family versus the evidence of his own senses.

chapters.title: What Ivo Was For
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV (rendered strangely, half-childlike). Ivo remembers being invented by twins in 1990s summers, remembers being real once, remembers the bargain the Eriksens made in 1974 that made room for things like him. Beat: sympathy for the monster-adjacent; Ivo loved the children more than the family did.

chapters.title: The Well Behind the Barn
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Ivo leads him to the dry well, capped with a stone carved with the family name. The stone is cracked open from the inside. Cold air rises carrying the smell of paint and turpentine. Beat: the past is not buried; it is waiting to be returned to.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, reading great-uncle Aldous's letters found in the attic. In 1974, Aldous painted a portrait of a neighbor boy who had drowned; the painting let the boy come back, but something else came back wearing his likeness. The family fed it, hid it, called it kin. Beat: horror of inherited complicity.

chapters.title: Wren, Resting
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He finally opens the locked east bedroom and finds Wren — or the thing using her — sitting in the dark, reciting their shared childhood verbatim, including moments only Wren could know. It asks him to stay forever. Part of him wants to say yes. Beat: longing weaponized.

chapters.title: Tally Marks
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He counts the tallies in his notebook: one for each day since the funeral, plus hundreds he doesn't remember writing. Ivo admits the house has been counting down to the harvest moon for decades, and every generation an Eriksen 'comes home so soon.' Beat: the trap has been set long before him.

chapters.title: The Portrait
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Behind the attic plaster he finds the 1974 portrait: the drowned boy, painted so lovingly it seems to breathe. On the frame's back, a name is written in Aldous's hand — and beneath it, a second name, fresher: WREN. Beat: understanding arrives; the painting is a door, and doors swing both ways.

chapters.title: Mother's Confession
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Confronted, his mother finally breaks: she knew the casket held no one, knew Wren was taken, chose the lie because the thing keeps the farm alive and the family together. 'Belonging costs,' she says. Beat: the theme stated outright — loyalty vs. truth, and the price of each.

chapters.title: Ivo's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo confesses he was the family's first returned thing, sent back in 1974 to watch the children, and that he warned them away from the well for years out of love. Returning the portrait will unmake him too. Beat: sacrifice foreshadowed; loyalty tested against truth from the other side.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises Early
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Clouds part days ahead of schedule — the house has been bending time, and the moon is nearly full tonight. The walls go silent, which is worse than noise. Every door in the house now opens onto the same hallway. Beat: the clock runs out; no more preparation, only choice.

chapters.title: Everything Wren Ever Said
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The thing wearing Wren floods the house with perfect memories, offering to be his sister, his twin, his whole lost family, if he only lets it stay. He almost signs the ledger it produces — the same ledger Aldous signed in 1974. Beat: climax of temptation; identity offered as a gift that is actually a cage.

chapters.title: The Name on the Back
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He realizes the second name under WREN is his own, freshly inked, dated tomorrow. The thing doesn't want consent — it wants substitution. Ivo tears the ledger from his hands, buying seconds with his unraveling form. Beat: betrayal revealed; the stakes become existential.

chapters.title: Carrying the Portrait
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. He runs the portrait through a house that has folded into a single endless hallway, pursued by everything the family ever pretended was normal. Mother stands at the far door, weeping, holding it shut against him — or holding it open? Beat: pure chase tension; loyalty literally barring the way to truth.

chapters.title: At the Well
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the cracked capstone, the thing wearing Wren catches him and speaks with her true voice one last time: 'Do it. Please.' He lowers the portrait into the well as the harvest moon crests. Beat: climax; the act of return performed at maximum cost.

chapters.title: Unmaking
chapters.summary: Alternating Xanthe/Ivo POV. The house exhales. Walls straighten, doors forget each other, the tally marks fade. Ivo comes apart gently in Xanthe's arms, thanking him for remembering him truly at last. Beat: catharsis; truth dissolves the haunting, and love survives the loss of the lie.

chapters.title: Two Graves
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. They bury the empty casket beside a second, older grave marked ALDOUS ERIKSEN, 1974. His mother, diminished and human, asks if he'll stay. He says he'll stay long enough to tell the truth properly. Beat: quiet aftermath; belonging rebuilt on honesty instead of silence.

chapters.title: The Orchard in Spring
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, months later. Blossoms on trees that were dead for decades. He repaints the porch, leaves the east bedroom door open to sunlight. Sometimes he sets out three cups of coffee out of habit, then laughs and drinks all three. Beat: healing without forgetting; grief integrated.

chapters.title: A Friend at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, final chapter. At dusk, a small figure with button eyes waits at the property line — new-made, child-sized, waving shyly. Xanthe understands some friendships are given back, not taken. He waves, and does not invite it in, and sleeps soundly. Beat: bittersweet resolution; the door stays closed, but kindness remains.
